result.summary: Hesiod continues the genealogy of the early gods. Night bears Doom, Fates, Death, Sleep and many afflictions, and Strife bears Toil, Oath and other evils. The sea-line of Nereus, Thaumas, Phorcys and Ceto produces the Nereids, Harpies, Graiae, Gorgons and the monstrous brood of Echidna, many slain later by heroes.

scenes.title: Heaven names the Titans
scenes.summary: Heaven calls his sons Titans in reproach, warning that vengeance will follow their deed.

scenes.title: Children of Night and Strife
scenes.summary: Night bears Doom, Fate, Death, Sleep, Dreams, the Fates, Nemesis and others; Strife bears Toil, Oath and many evils.

scenes.title: Nereus and his daughters
scenes.summary: Sea begets Nereus, Thaumas, Phorcys, Ceto and Eurybia. Nereus and Doris have fifty daughters; Thaumas and Electra have Iris and the Harpies.

scenes.title: Graiae, Gorgons and Geryones
scenes.summary: Ceto bears the Graiae and Gorgons. Medusa bears Chrysaor and Pegasus when Perseus beheads her; Heracles later kills Chrysaor's son Geryones.
scenes.stakes: Medusa suffers a woeful fate; Geryones is slain defending his oxen.

scenes.title: Echidna in her cave
scenes.summary: Echidna, half nymph and half snake, lives in a cave in Arima, placed there by the gods.

scenes.title: Monstrous brood of Echidna
scenes.summary: Echidna and Typhaon produce Orthus, Cerberus, the Hydra, Chimaera, the Sphinx and the Nemean lion; heroes and gods' plans bring many to ruin.
scenes.stakes: The monsters are destroyed by Heracles, Bellerophon and others.

analysis.text: The genealogy turns abstract forces such as Doom, Strife and Oath into divine beings, showing how Hesiod organizes the world's hardships as the offspring of Night and Strife.
Sea's descendants lead to monsters later defeated by heroes, linking the divine order to the heroic age.

legacy.text: The Hesiodic monsters, Cerberus, the Hydra, Chimaera and the Sphinx, became staples of Greek art, and the word chimera passed into English for an illusory or hybrid thing.

fun_facts.text: The 'Hesperides' and 'Harpies' here are early literary attestations; Hesiod's list of fifty Nereids is one of the longest name catalogs in Greek poetry.

language_notes.text: "Titans" is explained by Hesiod as derived from a Greek verb meaning "to strain"; the etymology is ancient and doubtful, but it frames the name as a reproach.
Destinies and Fates are the Moirai, who assign each person's portion of good and evil; the three named spin, measure and cut the thread of life.
Nemesis means righteous indignation or retribution, especially against those who have undeserved good fortune or who overstep their bounds.
"The Old Man" is a traditional title for Nereus, a sea god, reflecting his age and wisdom; he is truthful and does not lie.
"The Dark-haired One" is an epithet for Poseidon, who is the father of Pegasus and Chrysaor, though he is not named here.
Hesiod derives the names by wordplay: Pegasus from Greek pegai (springs), Chrysaor from aor (blade, sword) with chrysos (gold).
Heracles' tenth labour was to fetch the cattle of Geryones from the far west and drive them to Tiryns.
The Cadmeans are the people of Thebes, founded by Cadmus; the Sphinx plagued the city until Oedipus solved her riddle.

context_notes.text: The Hesperides were nymphs of the far west who tended a garden of golden apples, which Heracles later had to fetch.
The Graiae ("grey ones") are sisters who share one eye and one tooth in later myth. The Gorgons' glance turns people to stone.
Pegasus, the winged horse, serves Zeus by carrying his thunderbolts, as the text says.
The Hydra of Lerna was a many-headed water serpent. Heracles killed it as one of his labours, with help from his nephew Iolaus.
Bellerophon, riding Pegasus, killed the Chimaera, a task set for him by a king hoping he would die.

literary_notes.text: The Fates are goddesses who pursue wrongdoers and grow angry, giving abstract destiny and punishment a divine, vengeful will.
The long list of Strife's offspring, mostly abstract evils, builds a sense of strife's wide, destructive reach.
Nereus is defined by truthfulness, gentleness and justice, making him a moral contrast to the evil offspring of Night and Strife.
Repeated descriptors such as "rosy-armed" and "lovely" give the long list of Nereids rhythm and a sense of beauty.
The Harpies are said to be "quick as time," comparing their speed to the swift passing of time itself.
Echidna's divided body, lovely nymph above and speckled snake below, creates a vivid, unsettling picture of beauty joined with horror.
The Chimaera's lion, goat and dragon parts, together with fire-breathing, give a concrete, terrifying picture of a composite monster.
